title: KQL: filters, strings & columns
subtitle: Read a pipeline, preserve its schema, and choose the right string comparison.
intro: Kusto Query Language turns security telemetry into evidence. A pipeline begins with a table or tabular expression; each pipe passes its result into the next operator. The output of one step is the entire input available to the next. This matters when constructing a query from code blocks: a sensible operator can still be in the wrong place. Build a habit of asking three questions after every line: which rows remain, which columns remain, and what does one row now represent? The exam tests these decisions inside investigations and detections, not simply whether you recognize an operator name.

sections.title: Select rows before shaping the evidence
sections.body: Use where to retain rows satisfying a Boolean condition. Combine requirements with and; use or for alternatives and parentheses to make precedence explicit. Filter on an event time and specific entity early when those restrictions preserve the question you are asking. A result containing zero rows is not proof that activity never occurred: first validate the table, time window, permissions, and collection. Table and column names are case sensitive. Use the schema pane and inspect a few records before assuming that two products use identical field names.
sections.code:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where FileName =~ "powershell.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, FileName, ProcessCommandLine

sections.title: Whole terms, substrings, and equality
sections.body: The equality operator == is case sensitive; =~ compares entire strings without case sensitivity. The has family looks for alphanumeric terms, while contains looks for arbitrary substrings. For a command-line token such as DownloadString, has can be suitable when the token appears as a complete term. For a fragment inside a longer identifier, contains is the relevant semantic choice. has is generally more efficient for indexed terms, but performance does not justify changing the required meaning. A filename containing punctuation can split into several terms, so do not treat term matching as exact filename equality.

sections.title: Keep the columns that later steps need
sections.body: project chooses the output columns and can also rename or calculate them; any unlisted columns disappear. extend adds or updates calculated columns while retaining the other columns. Neither operator inherently groups events. If you project only DeviceName and then filter Timestamp, the time column is no longer available. Work backward from the required answer: keep correlation keys and evidence identifiers until the join or detection consumes them. At the end, shape a concise result with enough provenance for investigation. Avoid using take as a guarantee of the latest events; sort or top must express the desired ranking.

remember: where filters rows; project shapes columns; extend adds calculations.
== is exact and case sensitive; =~ is whole-string case insensitive.
has matches terms; contains matches substrings.
A column dropped by project cannot be used later without being recreated.
pitfalls: Do not confuse Kusto Query Language with the separate Keyword Query Language used in some content searches.
Faster matching is useful only if its semantics match the requirement.

title: KQL: counts, sets & latest evidence
subtitle: Control grouping and avoid losing the event that explains a finding.
intro: A SOC rarely needs an unbounded list of every log entry. It needs the users with repeated failures, hosts with many destinations, or the latest evidence for each device. Aggregation changes the meaning of a row: after summarize, a row describes a group rather than an individual event. Exam questions often hide this change inside a mostly correct query. Identify the required grain before choosing the by clause. Ask whether the requirement counts events, unique values, conditional events, or the complete record with the largest timestamp. Those are different questions and require different expressions.

sections.title: Event counts versus distinct values
sections.body: count() counts input records in a group. countif(predicate) counts records satisfying a condition within that group, allowing successes and failures to be measured together. dcount(column) estimates the number of distinct values rather than the number of rows; its approximation is appropriate when explicitly acceptable. A host with 500 connections to one IP has 500 events but one distinct destination. A detection for password spraying usually asks about many accounts from one origin, while brute force can involve many attempts against one account. The grouping keys determine which behavior the query describes.
sections.code:
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType != "0"
| summarize Failures=count(),
            Users=dcount(UserPrincipalName) by IPAddress
| where Failures >= 20 and Users >= 10

sections.title: Return the record that explains the maximum
sections.body: max(Timestamp) returns a scalar maximum for each group. arg_max(Timestamp, *) returns a row associated with the maximum and includes the selected evidence columns. Use it when the latest status must stay attached to its device or account. Independently aggregating max(Timestamp) and take_any(ReportId) can combine values from different events and produce false provenance. If multiple records tie on the maximum, do not assume an undocumented tie-break order. Add an explicit business rule if the distinction matters. Preserve the original event identifiers when preparing output for downstream investigation.

sections.title: Turn many values into useful evidence
sections.body: make_set produces a dynamic collection of distinct values; it is useful for listing the destinations associated with a finding. It does not provide chronological order. A grouped row containing an array is not one row per array member: use expansion later when that is required. Keep the list bounded to operationally useful evidence instead of collecting every high-cardinality field. An aggregation should answer a question that you can state in one sentence. If adding UserPrincipalName to the grouping unexpectedly removes a password-spray finding, inspect whether you split a source-wide pattern into small per-user groups.

remember: Choose the grouping keys before the aggregation function.
count is row count; countif is conditional count; dcount estimates unique values.
arg_max can retain a complete latest record.
make_set produces distinct values, without a promised ordering.
pitfalls: The group key can change an otherwise correct detection into a different detection.
Separately aggregating identifiers can detach them from the event timestamp.

options: by IPAddress

explanations: Grouping by origin preserves all targeted users for that origin.

options: make_set sorts by event time automatically.

title: KQL: time windows & network scope
subtitle: Build reliable time filters, bucket patterns, and interpret CIDR correctly.
intro: A technically valid query can still miss an attack because it asks for the wrong time interval or groups network events incorrectly. Hunting often uses a rolling relative window; incident reconstruction may require fixed UTC boundaries. Trend analysis needs buckets rather than one group per exact timestamp. Network investigations also require understanding which endpoint initiated a connection and whether an address belongs to a specified range. The exam can combine these fundamentals with KQL selection or code ordering. Read the requested time boundary literally, distinguish event time from ingestion delay, and trace the direction of each connection before attributing activity.

sections.title: Relative windows and fixed boundaries
sections.body: ago(1h) evaluates to a datetime one hour before the current UTC time. A predicate such as Timestamp > ago(1h) keeps recent events, while Timestamp < ago(1h) selects older events. between includes both boundaries. For adjacent fixed processing windows, a half-open interval using >= Start and < End avoids counting the exact boundary twice. The portal display timezone does not change the meaning of a UTC KQL timestamp. When investigating historical incidents, fixed datetime boundaries make the evidence reproducible, unlike a relative window that moves every time you rerun the query.

sections.title: Time buckets expose patterns
sections.body: bin(TimeGenerated, 5m) rounds timestamps down to five-minute boundaries so summarize can aggregate events in each interval. Without bin, grouping by an exact timestamp can leave nearly every event separate. Buckets describe discrete intervals; a burst straddling a boundary can be split across two buckets. Therefore a bucketed count is not identical to a continuously sliding-window detector. Validate the chosen window against the behavior you want to find. A larger hunting lookback also does not guarantee access to older data: retention and the selected data tier still govern availability.

sections.title: Interpret addresses before drawing conclusions
sections.body: CIDR defines a network prefix, not a textual prefix. ipv4_is_in_range(IP, "10.20.0.0/16") tests membership in the specified IPv4 network. A naive startswith check can confuse address boundaries. In endpoint network telemetry, RemoteIP and RemotePort describe the remote side, while initiating-process fields identify the local process responsible for the event. A connection to port 443 is useful context but does not establish that traffic is benign. Correlate address, process, identity, time, and destination context before deciding whether a connection is command and control or routine business traffic.

remember: ago returns a datetime relative to current UTC time.
between is inclusive; >= Start and < End creates a half-open window.
bin groups timestamps into discrete boundaries.
CIDR membership requires address-aware logic, not a substring match.
pitfalls: A five-minute bucket is not the same as every possible five-minute sliding interval.
Common ports do not prove benign traffic.

explanations: A text prefix can include unintended networks such as 10.21.

questions.stem: A burst consists of four events at 10:04:58 and four at 10:05:02. A query requires count() >= 8 by bin(Timestamp, 5m). Why does it not find the burst?

count ignores network records.

title: KQL: joins, unions & exclusions
subtitle: Correlate entities without silently losing or multiplying evidence.
intro: An investigation becomes useful when separate signals can be connected: a suspicious user to a device, a process to its network activity, or a destination to an indicator. A join combines matching records horizontally; union appends rows into a combined stream. The correct join flavor depends on what must happen to unmatched rows. A second, subtler decision is multiplicity: matching keys can produce many output pairs. Exam scenarios often require preserving all events, keeping unmatched assets, or identifying what has never matched. State the requirement in plain language before translating it into a join.

sections.title: Match the join to the question
sections.body: inner returns matching pairs from both sides. leftouter keeps every left record, adding matching right-side details when available. leftanti returns left records with no matching right record; use it for exclusions or missing coverage. Choose the table on the left deliberately because these semantics are directional. When key names differ, express the condition with $left.Column == $right.OtherColumn. A correlation key must identify the same real-world thing on both sides: matching an account display name to a device name merely because both are strings is meaningless.
sections.code:
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| join kind=leftanti (
    _GetWatchlist("ApprovedDestinations")
    | project AllowedIP=SearchKey
  ) on $left.RemoteIP == $right.AllowedIP

sections.title: Know the default and preserve multiplicity
sections.body: Kusto defaults to innerunique when the kind is omitted. That flavor deduplicates the left side by join key before matching. It can be useful for correlation, but it can also discard distinct left-side events that share a key. Use kind=inner explicitly when every matching event pair must survive. If three left records and two right records share a key, an inner join produces six pairs. Narrow time windows, deduplicate reference lists appropriately, and include more specific keys where available. Joining two process datasets solely on a reusable PID can create false matches; device and process-creation context matter.

sections.title: Append streams rather than invent relationships
sections.body: union combines rows from input tables rather than correlating their keys. Its default outer schema retains the columns from the inputs, leaving missing values when a source lacks a column. withsource can identify the source table. Align fields with project or extend when the same entity has different column names. A union of process and network tables does not prove a process caused a connection; that requires a valid key relationship. For small reference enrichment, lookup offers inner or leftouter behavior and assumes a smaller right-side dimension; do not use an enormous unfiltered reference as if it were free.

remember: inner: matches; leftouter: all left; leftanti: unmatched left.
Omitted join kind means innerunique, which deduplicates left keys.
union appends records; it does not correlate entities.
Repeated keys can multiply rows.
pitfalls: A key with matching data type is not necessarily a valid entity key.
Do not join endpoint process events on PID alone across devices and time.

questions.context:
CASE 3 — TAILSPIN HUNT

Tailspin is testing the hypothesis that users with repeated failed Entra sign-ins also start suspicious PowerShell processes on endpoints. SigninLogs contains TimeGenerated, UserId, and ResultType; "0" means a successful sign-in for this exercise. DeviceProcessEvents contains Timestamp, AccountObjectId, DeviceId, FileName, and ProcessCommandLine. In this dataset, AccountObjectId and UserId are populated with matching Entra object identifiers.

The hunt defines a suspicious user as one with at least ten failed sign-in records in the last hour. For each matching user, investigators want every matching PowerShell process event from the same hour, even if several events share the same user identifier. They must retain device and command-line evidence. A match tests the stated hypothesis; it does not by itself prove that the failed sign-ins caused the process execution.

title: KQL: JSON, expansion & reusable queries
subtitle: Extract nested evidence and build repeatable investigation logic.
intro: Security events frequently hide important properties inside JSON or dynamic arrays. An alert can mention several entities, a sign-in can contain nested status information, and an event can carry additional attributes not exposed as simple columns. Reading those structures correctly is necessary for both investigation and detection. Reusable query definitions also make complex investigations manageable, but a name is not automatically a cached result. The exam may ask you to choose parsing, expansion, casting, or query-building blocks. Follow the data type and row count through each transformation rather than treating JSON as ordinary searchable text.

sections.title: Parse and cast the property you need
sections.body: parse_json interprets a JSON string as a dynamic value; an existing dynamic value passes through unchanged. Access nested properties with dot or bracket notation, then cast to the scalar type the next operator needs, such as tostring or toint. Searching a serialized blob with contains can match the wrong property or value. If a property itself contains an escaped JSON string, parse that inner string separately; convert the inner dynamic representation to string before parsing again. Invalid JSON does not magically become a correctly structured object, so inspect representative data and handle missing values explicitly.
sections.code:
datatable(Payload:string)
['{"status":{"code":5},"entities":["u1","u2"]}']
| extend Parsed=parse_json(Payload)
| extend Code=toint(Parsed.status.code)
| mv-expand Entity=Parsed.entities
| project Code, Entity=tostring(Entity)

sections.title: Expansion changes the number of rows
sections.body: mv-expand emits rows for values in a dynamic array or property bag and repeats the other columns for each expanded element. A single alert containing three entities can therefore become three rows. This is useful for entity-level filtering or joins, but a later count now counts expanded records, not necessarily distinct alerts. Keep an alert identifier and use an appropriate distinct calculation when counting alerts. with_itemindex can retain element positions when position is meaningful. The type annotation on mv-expand is a cast, not a general parser for arbitrary element strings.

sections.title: Reuse a definition or cache a result deliberately
sections.body: A let statement binds a name to an expression and ends with a semicolon. You can define a scalar threshold, a time boundary, a tabular expression, or a reusable function. Reusing a named expression can cause it to be evaluated more than once. materialize captures a tabular result for reuse during that query execution, which can help expensive shared subqueries or nondeterministic expressions. It is not persistent storage, a scheduled job, or a guarantee of improved performance. Reduce data before materialization when semantics permit and compare actual runtime; caching an unnecessarily large result can worsen memory use.

remember: Parse JSON, access the intended property, and cast it to the required type.
mv-expand can multiply rows and duplicate parent-level fields.
let ends with a semicolon and defines an expression.
materialize caches a tabular result only for the query execution.
pitfalls: Counting expanded rows can overcount alerts.
let does not guarantee single evaluation of an expensive subquery.

questions.stem: Payload is a JSON string with a numeric nested status.code. You need a scalar integer for comparison. Which expression fits?

Payload contains "code"

questions.stem: Two branches reuse a costly tabular subquery that includes a nondeterministic calculation. You need the same evaluated result in both branches during one execution. What should you use?

let Shared = materialize(...); then reference Shared.

questions.stem: Starting from a JSON string Payload with an entities array, arrange the blocks to output one scalar entity identifier per row.
options: | mv-expand Entity=Parsed.entities
datatable(Payload:string) ['{"entities":["u1","u2"]}']
| project EntityId=tostring(Entity)
| extend Parsed=parse_json(Payload)

The datatable provides the input record.
Convert each expanded value and return the final field.
Parsing makes the entities array addressable.

title: Advanced hunting: choose the right table
subtitle: Map evidence to telemetry and correlate mail, identity, and endpoint activity.
intro: Before writing a clever query, find the data that can answer the investigation question. An alert table describes detections; a raw event table describes recorded activity; an inventory table describes an asset or software state. Those are different kinds of evidence. Advanced hunting combines Microsoft security services and, in the unified portal, connected Sentinel data, but table availability still depends on deployment, ingestion, retention, and access. Exam questions commonly ask which table or join key can prove a particular behavior. Learn the table families and the purpose of their important columns, then verify exact schemas in the built-in reference.

sections.title: Endpoint activity and inventory have different purposes
sections.body: DeviceProcessEvents records process creation and related activity. DeviceNetworkEvents covers connections; DeviceFileEvents covers file-system activity; DeviceRegistryEvents covers registry activity; DeviceLogonEvents covers authentication on devices. DeviceInfo describes device properties rather than every event. DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities and its knowledge-base partner support vulnerability questions. InitiatingProcess fields describe the process responsible for an event, whereas FileName in a process-creation event identifies the new process. Keep device identity, event time, and process-creation context when correlating. An empty network table can indicate missing service coverage rather than a clean environment.

sections.title: Mail evidence: message, attachment, URL, and click
sections.body: EmailEvents describes message processing, recipients, and delivery. EmailAttachmentInfo describes attachments; EmailUrlInfo describes URLs found in messages and attachments; UrlClickEvents describes Safe Links click events. EmailPostDeliveryEvents records security events after delivery. Correlate message-level tables with NetworkMessageId and include recipient context when your question is recipient-specific. A URL appearing in a message is not proof of a user click. Likewise, a blocked click event is different from evidence that a user reached a malicious page. SenderFromAddress is the visible From identity; SenderMailFromAddress is the envelope sender, which can differ.
sections.code:
EmailUrlInfo
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where UrlDomain =~ "suspicious.example"
| join kind=inner (
    EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress, DeliveryAction
  ) on NetworkMessageId

sections.title: Identity, cloud, alert, and behavior context
sections.body: IdentityLogonEvents covers supported identity authentication activity; EntraIdSignInEvents covers Entra sign-in activity in the current XDR schema. Sentinel SigninLogs is a separate schema with TimeGenerated rather than an assumption that every source uses Timestamp. CloudAppEvents helps examine SaaS activity. AlertInfo provides alert metadata, while AlertEvidence associates alerts with entities. BehaviorInfo and BehaviorEntities support behavior investigation and can include lower-confidence or tuned signals. Select the table that records the required fact, then correlate to alerts when needed. A threat classification attached to an alert is not a substitute for reconstructing the actual event sequence.

remember: EmailUrlInfo proves URL presence; UrlClickEvents provides click evidence.
NetworkMessageId links email records; include recipient scope when necessary.
Timestamp and TimeGenerated are schema-specific.
Check telemetry coverage before interpreting an empty result.
pitfalls: Do not use inventory tables as a substitute for event history.
InitiatingProcess and newly created process fields describe different processes.

lab.title: Map one attack story to evidence

For each step, select the relevant email, identity, or device table from the schema reference.
Inspect correlation identifiers and time fields in your authorized environment.
Write one bounded join and explain which steps remain unproven.

questions.takeaway: UrlClickEvents records Safe Links clicks in supported workloads.

questions.stem: You must correlate a suspicious email with its recipients and embedded URLs. Choose TWO appropriate decisions.
options: Use NetworkMessageId to relate EmailEvents and EmailUrlInfo.
Keep RecipientEmailAddress when determining who received the message.
Join only on the visible subject and assume it is unique.
Treat any URL record as proof that every recipient clicked it.
explanations: The Microsoft-generated message identifier supports message-level correlation.
Recipient scope matters when a message has multiple recipients.
Subjects are neither unique identifiers nor trustworthy correlation keys.
URL presence does not prove recipient behavior.
questions.takeaway: The Microsoft-generated message identifier supports message-level correlation.

questions.stem: You need to identify which executable initiated an outbound network connection, including its command line. Where should you begin?
options: DeviceInfo OS properties
DeviceNetworkEvents initiating-process fields
EmailAttachmentInfo
A workbook screenshot
explanations: Inventory properties do not identify the process responsible for a specific connection.
Connection records include initiating-process context alongside remote endpoints.
Attachment metadata cannot establish the network initiator.
A visualization is not the underlying event source.
questions.takeaway: Connection records include initiating-process context alongside remote endpoints.

questions.stem: An XDR query using Timestamp works. Copying it to Sentinel SigninLogs fails because Timestamp is unresolved. What should you do?
options: Replace the source with AlertInfo without changing the question.
Inspect SigninLogs schema and use its TimeGenerated event-time column.
Remove all time filtering permanently.
Rename every tenant table to use Timestamp.
explanations: Alert metadata does not replace raw sign-in evidence.
Time columns depend on the table schema; adapt the query to the correct source.
Unbounded queries avoid neither schema mistakes nor performance problems.
You should adapt the query rather than attempt to rename system schemas.
questions.takeaway: Time columns depend on the table schema; adapt the query to the correct source.

title: Sentinel hunts, ASIM & watchlists
subtitle: Turn hypotheses into evidence and make hunts portable across data sources.
intro: A hunt starts with a testable hypothesis, not a promise that an alert already exists. For example: an attacker may be using rare outbound destinations after a risky sign-in. Select data that can support or refute that idea, investigate results, record findings, and decide whether a reliable detection should follow. Microsoft Sentinel provides hunting queries and structured hunts. Normalization helps the same logic operate across products, while watchlists add reference context such as sensitive accounts or approved destinations. The exam tests which tool fits the operational goal and how findings become durable evidence or detections.

sections.title: A saved hunt does not automatically become a detection
sections.body: Hunting queries retrieve evidence when run. Analytics rules provide recurring detection behavior and alert or incident configuration. Saving a query alone does not schedule a production alert. In the Sentinel-specific hunting experience, bookmarks retain selected findings with query context, tags, notes, and entity mappings; serious findings can be escalated to incidents. Current documentation says bookmarks are not available in the unified Advanced hunting interface, although the Sentinel-specific Hunting experience still supports them. Know which experience a scenario names. Preserve important context with the tools available there rather than assuming identical features across all query pages.

sections.title: Normalize behavior rather than vendor column names
sections.body: ASIM unifying parsers query sources using a shared schema. A DNS hunt can use _Im_Dns instead of separately coding each vendor table. Normalized fields such as SrcIpAddr and ResponseCodeName let the logic describe behavior across sources. Parser parameters can push time and other filters earlier, improving performance. Normalization does not create telemetry that was never ingested and does not imply every parser is enabled. When converting a query, change the source, field names, and relevant normalized values together. Replacing only a table name while retaining vendor-specific fields can produce an invalid or incorrect hunt.
sections.code:
_Im_Dns(starttime=ago(1d), responsecodename="NXDOMAIN")
| summarize Requests=count() by SrcIpAddr
| where Requests >= 100

sections.title: Reference context with watchlists
sections.body: A watchlist is reusable reference data, not a stream of security events. Choose a SearchKey suited to the intended lookup, such as an IP address or account identifier. _GetWatchlist("alias") retrieves a watchlist for KQL correlation. A leftouter enrichment can add business criticality without discarding unlisted entities; a leftanti join can exclude approved items. Validate the alias, workspace, key type, and case normalization if results are unexpected. Membership in an approved list is context, not an unconditional security verdict. An attacker can compromise an approved administrator or use an approved destination.

remember: Hypothesis → query → validate → document → respond or engineer detection.
ASIM changes sources, fields, and values into a normalized schema.
Use available parser parameters for efficient filtering.
Watchlists supply reference context through a chosen SearchKey.
pitfalls: A saved hunting query does not itself create recurring alerts.
Bookmark availability differs between Sentinel-specific Hunting and unified Advanced hunting.

lab.title: Normalize and enrich a hunt
steps: Use an official Sentinel hunting exercise or your authorized lab.
Write a hypothesis and identify the data needed to test it.
Compare a vendor-specific query with an ASIM unifying parser query.
Create a small approved-IP watchlist and enrich or exclude matches deliberately.
Document one finding and explain how a reliable recurring detection would differ.

Notifications are not the required normalized DNS event source.

questions.stem: You are converting a vendor-specific DNS query to ASIM. Choose TWO necessary design checks.
options: Use the correct normalized field names and values.
Pass available time and filter parameters into the parser.
Assume the parser synthesizes missing logs.

explanations: Normalized schema semantics must replace vendor-specific assumptions.
Parameters allow filtering before expensive parsing where supported.

questions.takeaway: Normalized schema semantics must replace vendor-specific assumptions.

questions.stem: You must add a Criticality label from an asset watchlist while retaining events for assets missing from the list. Which design fits?
options: leftouter enrichment using the relevant SearchKey
inner join and discard all unlisted assets
Use the watchlist as a continuous raw event feed
Delete the original asset key before matching
explanations: A leftouter enrichment retains all left-side events and adds matching reference attributes.
This loses unlisted assets contrary to the requirement.
Watchlists are reference datasets, not raw event collection.
The correlation key must remain available.
questions.takeaway: A leftouter enrichment retains all left-side events and adds matching reference attributes.

questions.stem: You saved a hunting query and now require scheduled alerting with entity mappings. What is the next design step?
options: Assume saving already enabled production alerts.
Create and configure an analytics rule using validated logic.
Only export the query text to a bookmark.
Change the chart type to a workbook.
explanations: Saving a hunt does not define recurring detection behavior.
A configured analytics rule supplies recurring detection and alert behavior.
Preserving evidence does not schedule alerts.
Visualization does not implement detection scheduling.
questions.takeaway: A configured analytics rule supplies recurring detection and alert behavior.

title: Threat analytics & relationship graphs
subtitle: Prioritize relevant threats and distinguish observed attacks from possible reach.
intro: Threat intelligence becomes valuable when it changes an investigation or mitigation decision. Defender threat analytics combines researcher context with information about organizational impact and exposure. Graphs add another lens: entities become nodes and relationships become edges, making complex access and activity paths easier to inspect. The exam can ask you to interpret a report, choose a hunting pivot, or analyze the possible blast radius of a compromised entity. Keep observed compromise separate from potential future reach. A path to a sensitive asset is a reason to investigate and reduce exposure; it is not, by itself, proof that exfiltration already happened.

sections.title: Use reports to make a defensible priority decision
sections.body: Threat analytics reports provide narrative analysis, relevant detections and hunting queries, affected assets, exposure, and recommended actions. A newly published global threat can be less urgent for your organization than a slightly older threat with active incidents and many exposed critical devices. Use environmental context to prioritize. A hunting query in a report can supplement detections and reveal artifacts needing investigation; it does not label every result malicious automatically. Review the report scope and mitigations, then verify which controls are actually enabled in your environment. Recommendations are not proof those controls have already been applied.

sections.title: Hunting graphs and blast radius answer relationship questions
sections.body: The hunting graph in Advanced hunting helps traverse relationships among users, devices, and other assets. Blast radius extends incident analysis toward reachable critical assets and vulnerable paths from a compromised entity. These views help identify choke points and response priorities that a flat result list can obscure. Access depends on the relevant permissions and platform prerequisites, including Sentinel data lake and exposure-management access documented for the feature. When a graph is unexpectedly empty, examine data coverage and access rather than concluding the entity has no relationships. Validate suspicious paths against supporting activity and asset data.

sections.title: Understand the platform graph without overgeneralizing
sections.body: Sentinel Graph powers several relationship experiences across Microsoft security products. Custom graphs are a distinct preview capability that lets you model security data and publish materialized graph jobs, with graph querying after publication. An incident graph, an exposure path, and a custom graph are related experiences but are not interchangeable configuration objects. For the exam, focus on choosing graph analysis for cross-entity paths and understanding what nodes and edges represent. Do not confuse Sentinel Graph with Microsoft Graph API activity logs: one describes security relationships, while the latter records API access to Microsoft services.

remember: Prioritize threats using impact, exposure, and critical assets.
Hunting queries can reveal candidates needing validation.
Blast radius describes possible propagation toward critical assets.
Sentinel Graph and Microsoft Graph API logs serve different purposes.
pitfalls: Potential reach is not proof that an attacker traversed the path.
An empty graph can reflect missing access or source data.

Separate observed activity from possible exposure and identify a containment choke point.

options: No active incident proves the organization is safe.

Vulnerability or exposure is not proof of compromise.
Threat analytics can guide mitigation before detection.

options: Inspect the relationship and supporting telemetry before claiming access occurred.
Use the path to prioritize containment and reduce reachable exposure.

Ignore identity permissions because only device nodes matter.
explanations: A potential path needs evidence before it becomes an observed attack step.

A graph relationship alone does not prove data movement.
Identity access relationships are central to propagation analysis.
questions.takeaway: A potential path needs evidence before it becomes an observed attack step.

options: Hunting graph in Advanced hunting

Email notification recipients

explanations: The hunting graph visualizes and traverses security entity relationships.
Content search finds content rather than providing this asset relationship exploration.
Notifications do not expose propagation paths.

questions.takeaway: The hunting graph visualizes and traverses security entity relationships.

questions.stem: A manager asks whether a recommended mitigation in a threat report is already enforced in the tenant. What should you do?
options: Assume every recommendation was automatically deployed.
Validate the actual configuration and relevant exposure state.
Treat the report publication date as enforcement evidence.
Delete the report after reading it.
explanations: A recommendation is guidance, not evidence of enforcement.
Configuration and exposure evidence determine whether the mitigation is implemented.
Publication time does not prove tenant configuration.
Deleting context does not answer the control question.
questions.takeaway: Configuration and exposure evidence determine whether the mitigation is implemented.

title: Data lake jobs & summary tables
subtitle: Choose retrospective analysis, recurring aggregation, or single-table retrieval.
intro: Security teams need both fast current detections and economical historical investigations. The Sentinel data lake supports long-term analysis without treating every raw event as a hot analytics record. KQL jobs, summary rules, and search jobs solve related but different problems. A query that worked once in an editor is not automatically an operational pipeline: it needs the correct source tier, output destination, schedule, and monitoring. These newer capabilities are explicitly represented in the published SC-200 objectives. Learn the decision criteria and data flow, and verify current limits in the linked references instead of memorizing old product ceilings.

sections.title: Use KQL jobs for asynchronous lake investigations
sections.body: A KQL job runs a one-time or scheduled query against supported data lake and federated data. It is useful for historical correlation, indicator sweeps, enrichment, and analysis spanning several tables. Filter early and project only needed fields when promoting results to the analytics tier, since storing promoted output has cost implications. A job can write to a suitable output tier according to its configuration. Check onboarding, workspace access, source availability, and query support before scheduling. A request to join months of endpoint and identity history is a better match for a lake KQL job than a single-table search job.

sections.title: Use summary rules to precompute useful aggregates
sections.body: Summary rules periodically aggregate verbose data into custom Analytics-plan tables. Instead of repeatedly scanning all firewall events for a dashboard or detector, retain per-origin counts, first and last observations, and other required dimensions. The summary schema must preserve whatever the downstream question needs; discarded raw detail cannot be reconstructed from an aggregate. Configure query, destination table, bin schedule, and delay for ingestion latency. Preview the result before enabling the rule. Enable the relevant SummaryLogs diagnostics when operational monitoring is required and investigate failures using the diagnostic output.

sections.title: Manage the job lifecycle and choose the right alternative
sections.body: The Jobs page supports creating and managing KQL jobs, including enable or disable, history, editing, and deletion. Notebook and graph jobs are created in their authoring experiences and are view-only in the current Jobs page; change their query or schedule in the Sentinel VS Code extension and republish. Search jobs suit long-running retrieval from a single table and can bring historical results into an Analytics custom table. They do not replace a multi-table correlation job. If a downstream analytics rule needs recurring access to a summary, configure the detection separately: creating an aggregate table is not the same as creating an alert.

remember: KQL jobs: one-time or scheduled asynchronous historical analysis.
Summary rules: recurring aggregation into custom Analytics tables.
Search jobs: large single-table retrieval.
Monitor outputs and failures; aggregation alone does not create alerts.
pitfalls: A summary cannot restore raw columns you chose to discard.
Notebook and graph jobs are authored outside the general KQL job editor.

lab.title: Design a retrospective IOC sweep
steps: In an authorized lake-enabled lab, identify two retained tables and a bounded historical interval.
Draft a KQL correlation with a narrowly projected output.
Inspect the job destination and schedule before saving.

Inspect job history and the output table schema.

options: Edit and republish the notebook from the Sentinel VS Code extension.

Change a workbook parameter and assume the schedule follows.
Reinstall the email data connector.
explanations: Notebook jobs are edited in their authoring experience, not the view-only Jobs details.

The connector is unrelated to notebook job authoring.
questions.takeaway: Notebook jobs are edited in their authoring experience, not the view-only Jobs details.

options: Validate the summary table schema and execution health.
Choose the raw data and define required aggregate dimensions.
Configure and enable the summary query, output table, and schedule.
Create a separate analytics rule that queries the validated summary.
explanations: Validate what was produced before depending on it for alerting.
Start with the evidence and grain required downstream.
Configure the pipeline that produces the aggregate.
The detector is a distinct consumer of the summary data.
questions.takeaway: Start with the evidence and grain required downstream.

title: Notebooks & Sentinel MCP
subtitle: Choose reproducible Python analysis and connect AI tooling with the right access.
intro: Some investigations outgrow a single KQL result grid. You may need Python enrichment, custom visualizations, repeated transformations, or machine learning across a large historical dataset. A Jupyter notebook combines executable analysis, narrative, outputs, and evidence into a repeatable workflow. Sentinel now includes both established notebooks associated with Azure Machine Learning and data lake notebooks through the Sentinel VS Code extension. Model Context Protocol adds a structured connection between compatible AI clients and Sentinel tools. The exam focus is choosing the right workflow, understanding prerequisites, and interpreting results with evidence and permissions in mind.

sections.title: Know which notebook environment the scenario describes
sections.body: The established Sentinel notebook experience uses an Azure Machine Learning workspace and tools such as MSTICPy for data retrieval, enrichment, and security visualizations. It requires access to both the Sentinel data and the compute environment. Data lake notebooks use the Microsoft Sentinel VS Code extension and PySpark with managed Spark compute. These notebooks can transform large datasets and write selected outputs to supported lake or analytics tables. The two experiences have different setup steps; do not assume every notebook question requires creating an Azure Machine Learning workspace. Start from the named environment and the data it must process.

sections.title: Make analysis repeatable before automating it
sections.body: Document the hypothesis, sources, time bounds, transformations, and interpretation in notebook cells. Run cells in a known order because variables and intermediate state persist in the kernel; an apparently successful cell can depend on stale state from a previous run. Validate on a manageable sample, then scale the job and inspect output. Schedule lake notebook jobs from the supported authoring experience when recurring transformations or model scoring are needed. Save the analysis and evidence together so another analyst can understand which facts support the conclusion. A notebook is an analysis environment; it does not automatically create a production incident or prove causality.

sections.title: MCP connects a client to scoped security tools
sections.body: The hosted Sentinel MCP server exposes scenario-focused tools for data exploration, entity analysis, agent creation, triage, and hunting. Compatible clients connect using Microsoft Entra identity and the required permissions. In this model, VS Code can act as the host and maintain a client connection to the server. The server is not the notebook kernel and does not bypass data authorization. Distinguish an AI-generated explanation from its supporting query and retrieved evidence. Validate the time range and source coverage behind a natural-language result. A reliable workflow grants only the access needed for the investigation and reviews consequential response actions according to organizational procedure.

remember: Notebook combines code, narrative, results, and repeatable analysis.
Classic Azure ML notebooks and VS Code data lake notebooks have different prerequisites.
PySpark supports distributed lake analysis; MSTICPy supports security investigation workflows.
MCP is a client-server tool interface with Entra-backed access.
pitfalls: An AI result is not evidence unless its source and query support it.
Stale kernel state can make an analysis difficult to reproduce.

Run a small sample and restart or rerun the notebook in a known order.
If MCP access is available, connect a compatible client using the official setup guide and inspect retrieved evidence.

options: A lake notebook using the Sentinel VS Code extension and PySpark
Only a workbook title change

The analyst should validate the source data and time bounds behind the answer.

explanations: The server uses authenticated, permission-scoped access.

A tool interface does not bypass access controls.

questions.takeaway: The server uses authenticated, permission-scoped access.

questions.stem: A notebook succeeds only when cells were previously run in an unknown order. What is the strongest next step before scheduling it?
options: Document dependencies and validate execution from a clean kernel in the intended order.
Hide all code cells and trust the last chart.
Increase the font size.

explanations: A reproducible execution validates explicit dependencies and avoids hidden stale state.
Hiding code prevents review and does not fix dependency issues.

A scheduled execution needs complete explicit setup rather than stale interactive state.
questions.takeaway: A reproducible execution validates explicit dependencies and avoids hidden stale state.

questions.stem: An older tutorial says every Sentinel notebook requires an Azure Machine Learning workspace. A current task explicitly uses data lake notebooks in VS Code. How should you proceed?
options: Follow the current lake notebook prerequisites and supported Spark environment.
Create Azure ML solely because every notebook shares the same architecture.
Disable all data permissions.
Replace the notebook with an email notification.
explanations: The named notebook experience determines its setup and compute prerequisites.
Classic and lake notebook environments differ.
Permissions remain necessary for data access.
A notification does not perform the required analysis.
questions.takeaway: The named notebook experience determines its setup and compute prerequisites.
